title: *Redefining Global Health in the 21st Century* - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Cowen excerpts Reid and Goosby's Redefining Global Health in the 21st Century on 'fiscal substitution': donor health programs in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia crowded out domestic health spending, leaving externally managed systems vulnerable to funding shocks, with most countries never hitting their pledged 15% budget share for health. He closes by attacking the book's $150 Elsevier price as inconsistent with the authors' own pro-aid convictions.

insights.claim: Donor-funded health programs caused many governments in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia to scale back their own domestic health investment, as external money filled the gaps in HIV/AIDS, maternal and child health, and infectious disease control.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Aid does not simply add to health capacity; it displaces domestic budgets, so aid withdrawal produces a larger net hole than the headline donor number implies.
insights.quote: This phenomenon, often referred to as “fiscal substitution,” led to national health systems that were heavily donor-dependent, externally managed, and vulnerable to funding shocks.
insights.locator: While donor-driven programs undoubtedly saved millions

insights.claim: In some recipient countries domestic health budgets shrank in real terms even while external health funding was increasing.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Real-terms declines in domestic health spending during the aid boom mark exactly which countries are most exposed to a donor funding shock.
insights.quote: In some cases, domestic health budgets shrank in real terms, even as external funding increased.

insights.claim: Countries pledged to allocate at least 15% of their national budgets to health, yet more than two decades later only a handful have met that target.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A two-decade compliance failure on an explicit fiscal pledge is a hard prior against assuming domestic budgets will backfill withdrawn aid.
insights.quote: Notably, this reliance emerged despite countries pledged to allocate at least 15% of their national budgets to health.

insights.claim: Aid-built health systems became externally managed as well as externally funded, a governance dependency distinct from the money itself.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Rebuilding administrative capacity takes far longer than restoring a budget line, so aid-dependency unwinds are multi-year, not one-budget-cycle, adjustments.

themes.theme: Academic publishing rents versus aid rhetoric

insights.claim: Charging $150 for a slim academic volume through Elsevier is inconsistent with authors who advocate for aid, who could instead give the book away free.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Continued willingness of pro-aid academics to hand content to high-margin publishers shows the pricing power in legacy academic publishing remains intact despite open-access pressure.
insights.quote: But $150 for a not so thick volume!?
insights.locator: That is from the new and useful book
